David Leyonhjelm is the only libertarian senator in Australia, and leads the Liberal Democratic Party. He stands for personal and economic liberty and responsibility. Good write up here explaining quite honestly that the baby boomers should go fuck themselves, and why. He is a baby boomer himself.

I don't believe there has ever been a generation who has had it so good, and turned it so bad.
He is suggesting a big step backward. If his description of the current system is accurate, Australia should move forward into a system more like the American SSA system which works very well.

He is suggesting an end to middle and upper-middle class welfare, specifically for retirees. Can you explain how you think that's a step backwards? In my opinion, government assistance should only be given to those who actually need it. Not baby boomers with 7 figures of investments/superannuation holdings

Sure. Means-testing a benefit that is so widely needed complicates the system, promotes unequal application, and perhaps most importantly, costs far more in administrative expenses than having a universal system. Europe and the United States have nearly universal retirement systems whose costs are practically nothing.

Thanks for clarifying, but I disagree for a number of reasons.

Suggesting it's cheaper we pay everyone instead of means testing is ridiculous. Means testing does have administration costs, but you can't seriously suggest that it be cheaper than 10, 5 or even 2 years of pension payments. Hell I'd be surprised if it cost us more than 3 months worth of payments. And if it does that problem lies in the systems that the department of human services uses. (Anyone who has worked there can vouch for that, but I'm getting off topic)

You claim that old aged pensions are cheap? Are you sure about that?

Besides, giving taxpayer handouts kind of defeats the purpose of superannuation? There are exceptions to this of course, but I really don't think it'd be enough of a portion to justify this further drain on the Australian taxpayer.

Sounds more like you're an advocate for a universal payment/basic income/whatever it's being called these days?

Administrative costs (not program costs) for the nearly universal Social Security system in the United States, which does not means-test benefits, are well below one percent. Comparable means-tested programs begin at over five percent and increase sharply from there. That's about eight times the amount or more. It covers the lifetime benefits of over three million retirees.

While you are on the subject of program costs, SSA has a three trillion dollar accumulated surplus. There is no serious funding problem. For nearly 20 years, it has been consistently reported and widely accepted that an increase in the SSA tax of 0.9 percent would guarantee benefits for all indefinitely.

While much is made of the "SSA cap" and the fact that SSA taxes are flat or regressive, little attention is paid to the other side. SSA benefits are progressive. The lower your average income over the 35-year calculation period, the greater the percentage of average earnings you get. And it's a huge difference, running from 90 percent at the low end to just 15 percent at the high end. Those higher-earning workers that you think should be cut off are already receiving much lower returns on retirement benefits. They help to keep the program funded. IF you take that benefit away from them, it would be harder to justify the funding side.

Social Security is insurance. Insurance is not means-tested. Means-testing retirement benefits breaks the fundamental nature of the program. Perhaps that's exactly what this libertarian senator would like.

So as I started, Australia should adopt a system more like in America -- not splice, dice, and complicate their current system only to go backward. What Australia needs is a funded retirement insurance system.
